title: Diamagnetism
short_intro: Diamagnetism is a fundamental magnetic property exhibited by all materials in which induced magnetic moments oppose the applied magnetic field. It originates from the modification of orbital motion of atomic electrons under an external magnetic field according to Lenz's law.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of diamagnetic substances, negative and small magnetic susceptibility, relative permeability slightly less than one, independence of temperature (Curie-Weiss law non-applicability), and qualitative behavior in non-uniform magnetic fields (repulsion from stronger to weaker regions).
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Langevin's classical theory of diamagnetism, derivation of diamagnetic susceptibility using Larmor precession frequency, temperature independence proof, and quantitative calculations involving atomic number and mean square radius of electron orbits.

prerequisites: Atomic structure and electron orbital motion
Magnetic field intensity, magnetization, and magnetic susceptibility definitions

concept_notes.heading: Origin of Diamagnetism
bullets: Every material possesses diamagnetism because all atoms contain orbiting electrons that constitute microscopic current loops.
When an external magnetic field is applied, it induces an electromotive force via Faraday's law of induction.
According to Lenz's law, the induced current creates a magnetic moment that opposes the applied external magnetic field.

concept_notes.heading: Magnetic Susceptibility and Permeability
bullets: Diamagnetic materials have a small and negative magnetic susceptibility (χ), typically on the order of 10<sup>-5</sup> to 10<sup>-9</sup>.
The relative magnetic permeability (μ<sub>r</sub> = 1 + χ) is slightly less than unity.
The magnetic permeability (μ) of a diamagnetic substance is less than the permeability of free space (μ<sub>0</sub>).

concept_notes.heading: Temperature Independence
bullets: Unlike paramagnetism and ferromagnetism, diamagnetic susceptibility is independent of absolute temperature (T).
Thermal agitation does not disrupt the induced atomic currents because the induced magnetic moment is a direct dynamical response to the external field rather than an alignment of permanent dipoles.
Exceptions occur only in certain semimetals or superconductors where structural phase changes alter carrier density with temperature.

concept_notes.heading: Behavior in Magnetic Fields
bullets: When placed in a non-uniform magnetic field, diamagnetic materials move from regions of stronger magnetic field to regions of weaker magnetic field.
A freely suspended diamagnetic rod aligns itself perpendicular to the direction of a uniform magnetic field.
Superconductors exhibit perfect diamagnetism (Meissner effect), expelling all magnetic flux completely with χ = -1.

derivations.title: Langevin Theory of Diamagnetism
derivations.conditions: Spherical charge distribution of Z electrons per atom, weak external magnetic field B
steps: An electron of charge -e and mass m moving in a circular orbit of radius r experiences a change in angular frequency Δω equal to the Larmor frequency given by Δω = \frac{eB}{2m}.
This change in frequency induces an additional circular current i = -\frac{e Deltaomega}{2pi} = -\frac{e^2 B}{4pi m}.

The induced magnetic moment μ<sub>ind</sub> for a single electron orbit of area A = π<r<sup>2</sup>> is given by μ<sub>ind</sub> = i A = -\frac{e^2 B}{4pi m} pi <r<sup>2</sup>> = -\frac{e^2 B}{4m} <r<sup>2</sup>>, where <r<sup>2</sup>> is the mean square projection of the orbit perpendicular to the field.
Summing over Z electrons per atom and multiplying by the number density of atoms N gives the magnetization M = N ∑ μ<sub>ind</sub> = -\frac{Ne^2 Z <r<sup>2</sup>> B}{6m}.
Magnetic susceptibility χ = \frac{M}{H} = mu_0 \frac{M}{B} (since B ≈ mu_0 H for weak fields) yields the final diamagnetic susceptibility expression.

derivations.title: Behavior of Diamagnetic Rod in a Non-Uniform Field
derivations.conditions: Rod of volume V and susceptibility χ suspended in magnetic field gradient
steps: The potential energy U of a magnetic dipole of moment M in a magnetic field B is U = -M cdot B.
The induced magnetic moment per unit volume is I = χ H ≈ \frac{chi B}{mu_0}.
The total induced magnetic moment is M = V I = \frac{V chi B}{mu_0}.
Substituting M into the potential energy equation yields U = -\frac{V chi B^2}{mu_0}.

The force F acting on the rod along the field gradient is F = -\frac{dU}{ds} = \frac{V chi}{mu_0} \frac{d}{ds}(B^2). Since χ is negative, the force acts in the direction of decreasing magnetic field strength.
derivations.result: F = \frac{V chi}{mu_0} B \frac{dB}{ds} (pointing towards weaker field regions)

graphs_and_experiments.title: Magnetization (I) vs Magnetic Field Intensity (H)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight line passing through the origin in the fourth quadrant, with a negative slope equal to χ.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows that magnetization is directly proportional to applied field intensity but directed oppositely, resulting in negative susceptibility.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in MCQs to identify material type from I-H or M-H slope characteristics.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Susceptibility (χ) vs Temperature (T)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A horizontal straight line parallel to the temperature axis, indicating zero variation with T.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the complete temperature independence of diamagnetic susceptibility.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Differentiating diamagnetism from paramagnetism and ferromagnetism in conceptual questions.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Quincke's Method / Guoy's Balance Experiment Principle
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A U-tube setup showing depression of a liquid level or apparent weight loss of a diamagnetic sample placed between pole pieces of an electromagnet.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Measures the force exerted on a diamagnetic material in a magnetic field gradient to determine susceptibility.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Experimental basis questions regarding measurement of magnetic susceptibility in PGT exams.

solved_numericals.question: A diamagnetic substance has a magnetic susceptibility of -1.5 × 10<sup>-5</sup>. Calculate its relative permeability.
solution_steps: Recall the relation between relative permeability and magnetic susceptibility: μ<sub>r</sub> = 1 + χ.
Substitute the given value of susceptibility: μ<sub>r</sub> = 1 + (-1.5 × 10<sup>-5</sup>).

solved_numericals.question: Estimate the atomic diamagnetic susceptibility of a substance given that the atomic number density N = 5 × 10<sup>28</sup> m<sup>-3</sup>, Z = 10, and mean square radius <r<sup>2</sup>> = 1 × 10<sup>-20</sup> m<sup>2</sup>. Take μ<sub>0</sub> = 4π × 10<sup>-7</sup> T m A<sup>-1</sup>, e = 1.6 × 10<sup>-19</sup> C, m = 9.1 × 10<sup>-31</sup> kg.
solution_steps: Divide and evaluate: χ = -\frac{1.609 \times 10^{-7}}{5.46 \times 10^{-30}} \times 10^{-20} \text{ (re-evaluating powers carefully)} -> Let us compute directly: chi = - \frac{4pi \times 10^{-7} \times 5 \times 10^{28} \times 2.56 \times 10^{-38} \times 10 \times 10^{-20}}{5.46 \times 10^{-30}} = -1.96 \times 10^{-6}.

solved_numericals.question: A small bismuth sphere of volume 10<sup>-6</sup> m<sup>-3</sup> and magnetic susceptibility -1.6 × 10<sup>-5</sup> is placed in a non-uniform magnetic field where the product B(dB/dx) is 10<sup>2</sup> T<sup>2</sup> m<sup>-1</sup>. Calculate the magnetic force acting on the sphere. (μ<sub>0</sub> = 4π × 10<sup>-7</sup> T m A<sup>-1</sup>)
solution_steps: Use the force formula for a magnetic sample in a field gradient: F = \frac{V chi}{mu_0} B \frac{dB}{dx}.
Substitute V = 10<sup>-6</sup> m<sup>-3</sup>, χ = -1.6 × 10<sup>-5</sup>, B(dB/dx) = 10<sup>2</sup> T<sup>2</sup> m<sup>-1</sup>, and μ<sub>0</sub> = 4π × 10<sup>-7</sup>.
solved_numericals.answer: -1.27 × 10<sup>-3</sup> N (repulsive force away from higher field region)

assumptions_and_limitations: Langevin's classical theory assumes spherically symmetric electron charge distributions and independent atomic orbits, which is an approximation for multi-electron atoms in condensed matter.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Diamagnetism is absent in paramagnetic and ferromagnetic materials.
common_misconceptions.correct: Diamagnetism is an intrinsic property of all matter, but it is masked in paramagnetic and ferromagnetic substances because their positive paramagnetic or ferromagnetic responses are orders of magnitude larger.
common_misconceptions.why: All atoms contain orbiting electrons that undergo Larmor precession, but permanent atomic dipoles dominate when present.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Diamagnetic susceptibility depends strongly on temperature.
common_misconceptions.correct: Diamagnetic susceptibility is essentially independent of temperature.
common_misconceptions.why: Thermal motion does not affect the induced Larmor precession currents responsible for diamagnetism.

quick_revision: Diamagnetism is universal, temperature-independent, possesses negative susceptibility (χ < 0), relative permeability slightly less than one, and causes repulsion from strong magnetic field regions.
